name: higher-order-component
intent: Add cross-cutting behaviour to many components at once by wrapping them in an enhancer function that takes a component and returns a new, enhanced component, so no wrapped component knows about the concern or has to be edited.
problem: The same cross-cutting logic - subscribing to a data source, checking a permission, firing analytics, injecting a theme, a translation or a feature flag - is needed by many components, and copying it into each one couples every component to the concern, re-couples them to every change of it, and leaves the behaviour to be remembered at each new call site. React tried mixins and inheritance first and removed them (implicit dependencies between mixin and component, name clashes, snowballing coupling), so the recurring decision is how to apply one behaviour to many components without editing them, while the components stay reusable and unaware of the enhancement.
context: Component-model UI code where components are values the framework mounts with a stable identity (React and its ecosystem first; the same shape recurs with Compose composables, SwiftUI views, Blazor components, Scala.js layers and handler-based Go/Java web UIs), where the concern is genuinely cross-cutting rather than local to one screen, where the enhancement can be expressed as a pure function from component to component and applied once at the definition or export site, and where the wrapped component's inputs form a prop-like contract that can be extended by injection without touching its internals.
benefits: Written once, applied many times: the concern lives in one enhancer and is attached to components at their definition or export site, so no wrapped component contains it.

Purely functional composition: an enhancer is Component => Component, so single-argument enhancers compose with a tiny compose/flowRight helper and can be ordered, tested and reused like any other function.
The wrapped component stays independently usable and unaware - it only ever sees props, so the same component can ship enhanced, unenhanced or enhanced differently at another call site.
Enhancement works on components that cannot be edited: third-party and vendored components (connect, withTranslation, withRouter) are enhanced from the outside.
The enhancer owns the concern's state and lifecycle (subscription, timer, permission check, context read), which keeps those details out of every consumer component.
It reaches code that hooks cannot: logic can be shared into class components and into library APIs that must accept any component shape, where the hook-based alternative is unavailable.
tradeoffs: Wrapper hell: every enhancer adds a component node to the tree, so devtools trees, stack traces and statically analysable optimizations (for example the React Compiler) degrade as layers pile up - a custom hook adds none.
Invisible contract: what a component actually receives depends on enhancers applied elsewhere, usually at its export site, so its real inputs cannot be read from its own file.

Silent breakage at the wrapper boundary: refs and static members do not pass through a wrapper unless they are forwarded deliberately (forwardRef, hoist-non-react-statics), and an injected prop that collides with a parent-passed prop is decided by spread order rather than by the type system.
Identity trap: applying an enhancer inside the render path creates a new component type on every render, which unmounts and remounts the subtree and loses its state.

Typing is permissive: a generic enhancer needs gymnastics to preserve the wrapped component's props (ComponentType, Omit), externally supplied props are not enforced, and many mistakes surface only at runtime.

Two idioms in one codebase: the ecosystem moved to hooks for logic reuse, so enhancers persist mainly for libraries, class components and component-shaped wrappers, and teams end up maintaining both styles.
Debuggability is by convention: anonymous wrappers make enhanced components unrecognizable in devtools unless displayName is wrapped and the convention is actually followed.

participants.responsibility: A pure function of the wrapped component (optionally plus configuration) that returns the enhanced component; it owns the cross-cutting concern and must neither mutate nor inherit from the wrapped component.
The component being extended: it keeps its prop-based contract, contains no knowledge of the enhancer and stays usable on its own.
The component the framework mounts; it owns the concern's state and lifecycle, merges its injected props with the pass-through props and renders the wrapped component.
The values and callbacks the enhancer supplies (data, identity, permissions, flags, theme, tracking) plus the pass-through convention that lets unrelated props reach the wrapped component.
The single place where the enhancer is applied and ordered, individually or through compose; the only place where the wrapping is visible.
Mounts the enhanced component, keeps component identity stable across renders (which is why enhancers are applied outside render) and handles refs and ambient context.

use_cases: Subscribing many components to an external data source — React documentation's withSubscription example, or Redux's connect: store state arrives as injected props with no component knowing about the store.

Apollo Client data injection: graphql(Query, { options, props }) HOC maps query results and loading state to props; multiple graphql HOCs composed with @compose; historically the standard before useQuery.

Authorization and feature gating at the boundary: withAuthorization(Component, { requiredRole }) or withFeatureFlag(...) decides rendering without editing the component; useful for route-level guards applied across many pages.
Analytics, telemetry and instrumentation applied at export sites (withAnalytics): tracking calls stay out of presentation code and can be added or removed at one location per module.

Injecting ambient context into components that take it as props — translations via withTranslation (react-i18next), routing via withRouter (React Router v5 and below), theming via withTheme (Material-UI v4) — enabling third-party and vendored components to participate without modification.

Error and loading boundaries as an enhancer (withErrorBoundary): the boundary exists as a component in the tree anyway; an enhancer consolidates the concern into one reusable definition rather than repeating the try/catch at each call site.
Sharing logic into class components and older codebases where hooks cannot be used: the HOC reaches class components and library component-shaped APIs that hooks cannot wrap.
Material-UI v4 theming: withStyles and withTheme HOCs inject classes and theme as props; compose chains combine styling with data (connect + withStyles + graphql on the same export).
Internationalization testing: export both wrapped and unwrapped components; tests use the raw component with a mock t function while integration tests use the full I18nextProvider setup.
Conditional prop injection: a data-enhancer that only injects props when a condition is met (e.g. user is authenticated) lets the wrapped component remain agnostic about the absence of that data.

React Compiler (React Forget) compatibility: heavy HOC layering reduces the compiler's static analysis surface and may cause it to bailout — test compiler output when adding HOCs to a compiled codebase; prefer hooks for new logic the compiler should see.

React Server Components boundary: a HOC that calls hooks or reads client-only context (useAuth, useTheme, useRouter) cannot execute during a server render; the wrapped component may receive undefined injected props on the server and flash-change on hydration. Pass server-fetched data as props through the HOC boundary from a server parent instead.

Streaming SSR and Suspense integration: a HOC that wraps a component behind a Suspense boundary adds a node that may delay streaming; if the HOC itself is async it must be carefully placed to avoid blocking the fallback from showing.

Partial hydration patterns: on islands architectures (Next.js App Router, Astro), a HOC that subscribes to client-side state forces the entire island to be hydrated even if the wrapped component has no server payload; prefer passing hydrated state as props from a server parent.

Recompose (acdlite): a 'lodash for React' utility belt built entirely from composable HOCs (withState, mapProps, pure, branch) piped through enhance/compose - the pattern industrialised; its October 2018 deprecation in favour of Hooks (bug-fix maintenance only) is the canonical case study of the pattern's cost when a runtime offers a cheaper reuse primitive.

MobX React binding: observer from mobx-react / mobx-react-lite is an official HOC that subscribes the wrapped component to every observable read during render, re-rendering it automatically; MobX guidance is to apply observer first (innermost) when composing it with other HOCs, and to wrap every component that reads observables.
avoid_when: New function-component code with a small number of call sites: a custom hook (useX) is simpler - no extra node, no injected props, no ref/static/displayName bookkeeping - and the React documentation recommends it.
The shared thing is markup rather than behaviour: composition with children (<Card>{children}</Card>) beats withCard(...).

The behaviour has to be configured differently at every call site: a hook or an explicit parameter keeps the variation visible where it is used, while an enhancer configuration hides it behind the export site.
What is actually shared is state: context plus a hook (useAuth()) is clearer than injecting state through an enhancer.
Only one or two components need the behaviour: the extra wrapper, the identity and the indirection are never repaid.
The framework has no component identity to preserve (plain function composition in a render loop, a server-side template pipeline): an ordinary higher-order function or a decorator is enough.
anti_patterns: Mutating the wrapped component (patching its prototype or adding methods) instead of wrapping it: the result is a leaky, non-composable abstraction that clashes with every other enhancer and breaks on function components.
Applying an enhancer inside the render path, so every render produces a new component type and the framework remounts the subtree, dropping state and performance.
Silent prop shadowing: an injected prop that collides with a parent-passed prop of the same name, resolved only by spread order, without namespacing the injected props.
An authorization or feature-gate enhancer missing from one export path, so the guard silently does not run for that consumer.
Deep wrapper stacks (withRouter(withAuth(withTheme(withAnalytics(Component))))) sold as reuse where a hook or context would carry the same behaviour with no tree depth.
Claiming refs and static members survive wrapping without forwarding them (forwardRef, hoist-non-react-statics), turning a documented caveat into a production surprise.

React Compiler bailout: the compiler works best with statically analysable components. Heavy HOC layering hides logic behind opaque function calls, causing the compiler to bailout more often — defeating the purpose of adding it. Test compiler output when adding HOCs to a compiled codebase.

React Server Components incompatibility: any HOC that calls hooks or reads client-only context cannot execute during a server render. A component that assumes it receives injected props may render with undefined values on the server and flash-change on hydration; the fix (Client Component wrapper) is invisible to the wrapped component.

Generic component type erosion: wrapping a generic component (Table<T>) with a non-generic HOC drops the type parameter — Table<T> silently becomes Table<unknown> unless the HOC is itself generic (<T>) and passes T through. TypeScript may not flag this at the call site.

Strict Mode double-mounting: in React 18 StrictMode, components mount, unmount, and remount. A HOC that subscribes in useEffect will subscribe/unsubscribe/resubscribe, which is correct but can expose bugs in subscription libraries not designed for idempotent teardown.
design_principles: Composition over inheritance: enhance by wrapping the component, never by mutating it or inheriting from it.
Open/closed principle: a new behaviour arrives as a new enhancer applied at the export site, not as edits to the components.
Single responsibility: the enhancer owns the cross-cutting concern, the wrapped component owns rendering.
Pure functions and referential stability: enhancers are side-effect-free Component => Component functions applied once, so the enhanced component keeps one identity across renders.
Explicit boundary contract: injected props plus the pass-through convention are the interface, and refs, statics and optional interfaces must be forwarded deliberately.
best_practices: Apply enhancers at the module's definition or export site, never inside the render path; if the enhancement must be dynamic, apply it in a lifecycle method or the constructor, not per-render.
Keep the enhancer a pure function of its inputs: no mutation of the wrapped component and no side effects while the wrapper is being constructed.
Use single-argument enhancers (Component => Component) so they compose with compose/flowRight and their order is explicit and testable; configuration flows through a closure.
Namespace injected props (e.g. auth_user, analytics_event) or destructure and strip before spreading to avoid silent prop-shadowing collisions with parent-supplied props.
Wrap the display name (WithSubscription(CommentList)) so enhanced components stay identifiable in React DevTools; without it, anonymous wrappers are unreadable in the component tree.
Forward refs deliberately: use React.forwardRef in both the HOC signature and the wrapped component; in React 19+ refs can be passed as an ordinary prop but explicit forwarding is still the norm.
Hoist non-React static methods explicitly with hoist-non-react-statics (or manual Object.assign) instead of assuming they survive wrapping.

TypeScript: prefer generic HOCs constrained with T extends {} and ComponentType<T>, intersect injected props (T & InjectedProps), use Omit<P, keyof InjectedProps> to exclude injected props before forwarding, and cast remaining props as T when destructuring; for complex generic chains prefer LibraryManagedAttributes to align default props.

Testing: export both the raw component (for isolated unit tests) and the enhanced version (for integration tests); use WrappedComponent (enzyme) or direct import (RTL) to reach the inner component; for withRouter use MemoryRouter or createRoutesStub; for withTranslation provide a mock t via __mocks__/react-i18next.js or I18nextProvider.

Performance: be aware that each enhancer adds a component node to the tree — React Compiler optimization (autopratic) works through wrappers less effectively than through hooks; prefer React.memo on the wrapped component inside the enhancer rather than wrapping a bare component.

For TypeScript, avoid overly generic return types that collapse the wrapped component's prop interface; prefer explicit intersection types and test that the enhanced component rejects unknown props at compile time.

Prefer a custom hook for new function-component logic; reserve enhancers for library APIs (connect, graphql, withStyles, withTranslation), class components and component-shaped wrappers such as error boundaries.
When multiple enhancers are composed, document the prop namespace contract and the composition order because the order matters for injected props and lifecycle sequencing.

For React Server Components compatibility: only use HOCs that pass data as props in Client Components; never assume a HOC reading client context works during SSR. If the wrapped component needs server data, fetch it in a server component parent and pass it as props through the HOC boundary.

When using React Compiler: keep HOC layers shallow and test the compiler's output (React DevTools shows which components compile vs. bailout). If a critical path bails out, prefer a custom hook the compiler can see instead.

For generic component support: make the HOC itself generic (<T extends object>) and infer the wrapped component's type parameter. Use a second generic for injected props (InjectedProps extends object). The return type should be ComponentType<Omit<ComponentProps<T>, keyof InjectedProps> & InjectedProps>.

Compose aggressively: when more than two enhancers are applied, extract a module-level compose helper (compose = (...fns) => fns.reduceRight((acc, fn) => fn(acc))). Document the order and keep it stable — composition order matters for lifecycle sequencing and prop injection priority.
